title: How Online Dating Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore the history and practice of online dating. They trace computer matchmaking from Jeff Tarr's 1965 Operation Match at Harvard and Jeffrey Ullman's Great Expectations video dating service, through Match.com and JDate in the 1990s, to modern niche sites and apps like Tinder. They walk through the typical signup process (browsing, profile building, free vs. paid sites), tips for writing a good profile and first contact, safety advice such as meeting in public and verifying photos with reverse image search, and data-driven findings from OkCupid and Match.com about what profile content attracts dates. A listener email about robots replacing doctors closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and history of computer dating
segments.summary: The hosts joke about their own dating experience and the movie Singles, then trace computer dating from Jeff Tarr's Operation Match in the 1960s, through Jeffrey Ullman's Great Expectations video profiles, to the 1990s launch of Match.com and JDate. They discuss the stigma around online dating and its growth in the 2000s.

segments.title: Niche dating sites
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck list a range of niche dating sites, from general sites like eHarmony and Match to sites for specific interests, religions, politics, parents, cat lovers, and people with specific traits.

segments.title: Signing up and building a profile
segments.summary: The hosts walk through the basic online dating process: browsing without paying, entering minimal info, adding email and physical attributes, filling in interests and lifestyle details, and noting that many users lie about height, income, photos, and sexuality.

segments.title: Photos, safety and fake profiles
segments.summary: The hosts discuss keeping photos accurate, avoiding personal information like addresses or workplaces, and using reverse image search to spot scam or fake profiles. They contrast free sites, which attract impostors, with paid sites that verify identity.

segments.title: Writing a good profile
segments.summary: Drawing on advice from Ed Grabanowski, the hosts recommend specific, humorous, honest profile writing, a good photo, complete forms, and knowing what you want, and warn against halfhearted or lazy profiles and saying friends made you sign up.

segments.title: First contact, matching algorithms and browsing
segments.summary: The hosts discuss sending first messages, whether to message many people or a few, and how matching works: questionnaire comparison versus proprietary algorithms like eHarmony's dimensions and Chemistry.com's personality inventory developed by Helen Fisher. They note that self-reported preferences are unreliable and that stating deal-breakers clearly helps.

segments.title: Phone calls, first meetings and safety
segments.summary: The hosts advise talking by phone before meeting, keeping first dates public and short, and cite a Las Vegas lawsuit against Match.com after a fatal attack. They then cover mobile dating apps such as Tinder and data-driven tips from OkCupid and Match.com, as reported by Wired, about words, photos, and profile content that affect response rates.

segments.title: Listener mail: robots replacing doctors
segments.summary: A listener from Sacramento, Andy Ping, writes that doctors will not be replaced soon but that thinking machines might eventually replace them. The hosts thank him and give contact info.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to the Ed Grabanowski article, social media, email, and the show website, then close the episode.
